extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in the Steele dossier and Trump–Russia allegations
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the credibility and corroboration status of allegations in an intelligence dossier (the Steele dossier) by comparing them to official reports, intercepted communications, independent sources, and investigative findings. Emphasizes how corroboration, vetting, and methodology affect whether raw intelligence becomes analytic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by U.S. intelligence agencies and the Mueller report
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain allegations in the dossier have been publicly corroborated by U.S. intelligence agencies, the January 2017 ODNI report, and the Mueller report (for example: that the Russian government was working to get Mr. Trump elected; that Russia sought to cultivate people in Trump's orbit; that Trump campaign officials had secretive contacts with Russian officials; that Putin favored Trump; and that Putin ordered an influence campaign and cyberattacks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative confirmation from ODNI, the Mueller report, and intelligence community assessments as strong evidence that a dossier allegation is corroborated. The page lists specific claims that these sources have corroborated and treats such corroboration as substantially increasing confidence in those allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and rigor of FBI corroboration efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: The FBI's attempts to corroborate the dossier's allegations were criticized as lacking 'thoroughness and rigor' (the FBI focused on identifying Steele's source network and recruiting sources rather than full corroboration of all dossier claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims with attention to how comprehensively law enforcement/intelligence investigative steps were taken. A deficiency in thoroughness or rigor in official corroboration efforts weakens the evidentiary status of allegations; note the FBI's stated focus and the Senate Intelligence Committee's criticism when weighing credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple independent sources for corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: DOJ provided additional information obtained through multiple independent sources that corroborated Steele's reporting in FISA renewals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroboration that comes from multiple, independent lines of evidence is stronger. When assessing an allegation, prioritize information that is supported by independent sources rather than single-source claims or anonymous rumor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with intercepted communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Intercepted communications corroborated some conversations detailed in the dossier — confirming that certain conversations took place between the same individuals on the same days and from the same locations as described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match dossier claims against available communications intercepts, timestamps, and locations. Consistency across such concrete signals increases confidence in those items; such intercepts served as important corroborative evidence in the article's examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting requirement for inclusion in formal analytic judgments (ICA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CIA and other agencies resisted including dossier allegations in the body of the January 2017 ICA because the dossier 'was not completely vetted and did not merit inclusion in the body of the report'; only a short summary was added to a classified annex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inclusion in formal analytic judgments (like an ICA) as contingent on vetting. Material that has not passed agency vetting should not be treated as equal to vetted analytic judgments; absence from a public analytic judgment can reflect concerns about sources, methods, or corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating the dossier as raw intelligence rather than proven fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele and his associates described the dossier as 'raw intelligence' and cautioned that it was not proven fact; Simpson and Steele noted that 'nothing... disproves anything in the dossier' but also that they do not think all of it is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using the dossier, maintain a distinction between raw intelligence (leads, allegations, tips) and established facts. Weight claims accordingly: raw intelligence can guide investigation but requires corroboration before being reported as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility versus specific confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some allegations are described as 'plausible but not specifically confirmed'; others are 'dubious in retrospect but not strictly disproven'. Allegations may be untrue, unimportant, or too sensitive to confirm publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess allegations along an axis of plausibility and available confirmation. Do not conflate plausibility with confirmation; label plausible-but-unconfirmed allegations as such and note possibilities (untrue/insignificant/too-sensitive) that could prevent public corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate Committee's evaluative focus — methodology and source network
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate Intelligence Committee did not seek to prove or disprove dossier assertions; instead it 'explored Steele's methodology, explored the information available on Steele's subsources, examined how the FBI handled Steele as a source, and sought to understand how the FBI investigated the assertions in Steele's reporting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When auditing an intelligence product, prioritize scrutiny of collection methodology, source reliability, handling by consuming agencies, and investigative follow-up rather than attempting to adjudicate every allegation. The committee's approach exemplifies oversight focused on process rather than verdicts on individual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration can change with the passage of time and new public records
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses (e.g., Lawfare retrospective) found that after two years and the release of additional official records, some of Steele's reporting was buttressed while other parts remained uncorroborated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that corroboration status is dynamic. Reassess previously uncorroborated claims as new evidence (investigative records, indictments, intercepted communications, public reports) becomes available; update credibility judgments accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of corroboration by 'trustworthy and official government sources'
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawfare and other analysts used 'trustworthy and official government sources' to judge whether the dossier 'buttress[ed] some of Steele's reporting, both specifically and thematically.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater weight to corroboration that comes from credible, official, and transparent sources (e.g., declassified reports, official indictments, intelligence community assessments) when determining whether dossier material is supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiating types of evidence (intercepts/indictments vs rumor/media/video)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article contrasts strong corroborative items (intercepted communications, intelligence reports, Mueller findings, indictments) with weaker or unproven items (rumors, alleged videos, unverified innuendo such as the 'pee tape').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize evidence by type and inherent reliability. Treat intercepts, official reports, and legal findings as higher-quality corroboration than media-circulated rumors, anonymous videos, or hearsay. Label and caveat items of lower evidentiary quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of access to investigative equities limits public assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate Committee 'lost access to all relevant information regarding FBI's efforts to verify the dossier, as it did with all information the SCO declared to touch its
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When oversight or reviewers lose access to classified equities or investigative materials, public evaluation of corroboration is constrained; note such access limitations when judging whether allegations were or could be corroborated.
